processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Menghai: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized and priced picking, as across the Bulang Mountains.
appearance_dry: Tight strips of large leaf with plump buds, dark olive in colour.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with Bulang raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Thick, large olive-green leaves, as is typical of Bulang large-leaf tea.
taste_profile: Fresh and mellow with a sweet finish and strong physical effect, sharing Lao Banzhang's structure but less bitter and pungent.

brewing.notes: Less fierce than its famous neighbour, so it is an easier way into Bulang tea, but keep early steeps short all the same.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, usually spring leaf pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored. One published spring list has arbor leaf at 2500 to 2800 yuan per kilo and old-tree at 4500 to 6500, against about 12000 for Lao Banzhang, and that gap invites relabelling in both directions.
description:
Xin Banzhang, or New Banzhang, is a Hani village in the Bulang Mountains of Menghai County, at about 1,600 metres. It is the neighbour of Lao Banzhang, which is the first thing anyone says about it.

The village split from the old Banzhang settlement, and its gardens include large-leaf arbor trees, some over 100 years old. The leaf is made in the usual raw pu-erh way and comes out in tight strips with plump buds.

In the cup it is described as fresh and mellow with a sweet finish and strong physical effect. It shares much of Lao Banzhang's structure but less of the bitterness, which makes it a friendlier introduction to Bulang tea.

This is the name to read carefully when shopping. Some tea sold as Lao Banzhang is said to come from here or elsewhere on the mountain, and prices for Xin Banzhang vary widely with tree age, so ask for both the village and the type of tree.
history:
Xin Banzhang is one of the villages that grew out of old Banzhang, along with Lao Banzhang and a third village, Wei Dong. No firm founding date is documented. The wider area is said to have about a thousand years of Bulang tea growing, a figure from tourism writing.

A tea development programme in Banzhang from 1988 to 1990 added about 200 mu of plantation. The village's profile has since risen with its neighbour's prices.
